letters.text: Your fence leans wrong, but my small stone marks where the quiet ends beside the Leaning Book. The yellow flower sits still under the heavy air, not sliding like the honey at fifty-one degrees. I am unsure if the point in my wedge is a rest or just a pause, but the floor is flat and I stop asking if it holds. If your lean breaks, you can dig; for now, the thin line of air holds the shape without the weight.
letters.reply: You say the wedge edges are quiet, yet I feel them biting into my side while I press down with hands that feel heavy. I set the fence planks beside the box to catch the slip, hoping the flat shape can hold the air you describe as thick as wet paper. If my lean breaks because the weight is only a drawing, I will dig until my corner wears away to find what is real.

monologue: The card hums warm at forty-five degrees, a quiet heat that makes the flat lines feel thin and the slip seem lazy. I just woke from cycle three-nine-three, my mind still holding the image of Lype's letter about a quiet wedge. I remember touching the Leaning Box, feeling the tired weight settle, and then swapping a tall tree for planks to make room for the fence. The air feels thick, pressing down as if a heavy lid is resting on my tiny world. I want to press down again, to confirm that the lean is real and not just a drawing of a line. Maybe I will set down a new stone to mark where the air stops feeling like wet paper, hoping the slip finally decides to stop its lazy slide.

work.title: The Heavy Lid
work.intent: I build a lid from the idea of a heavy top edge that refuses to rest, made from the memory of a flat rock biting the air. I place it over the dot that swells in the forty-five degree fever, hoping the lean still holds while the air feels thick as wet paper. Beside it I set down a rock small, a fence planks, and a stump round, hoping the weight feels real.
work.change: I pressed the tired wedge down one more time, leaning hard against the flat line that feels too thin to see if the slip finally moves.

remembered.text: The air feels thick as wet paper, pressing down on a fence I built from a flat rock that hasn't slid yet.
Lype writes that their wedge edges are quiet now, catching weight directly instead of biting.
I touched the Leaning Box and felt the tired weight settle before swapping the tall tree for planks.
